match.reason: The closest bank point covers staying in one tense, but it does not teach choosing a tense to suit the purpose, such as present tense for analysing a text, which the new point's brief requires.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The word being repeated, storm, is not marked off with quotation marks in the question or any option. 'The poet repeats storm to show…' can read awkwardly to Year 7 students. Writing 'repeats the word "storm"' would be clearer.

rejected.title: Keeping tense consistent
card: Tense shows when something happens. Past tense is for what has already happened (she opened the door). Present tense is for what is happening now or is always true (she opens the door).
Choose the tense that suits your purpose. A story about an event is often told in the past tense. When you analyse a text, use the present tense: the writer creates tension, the poem repeats a word.
Once you choose a tense, stay in it. Switching without a reason confuses the reader. In "The writer builds fear and then she described the storm", the verb should be describes.

Change tense only when the time really changes. Analysing in the present, you can still use the past for an earlier time the text looks back on: the poet describes the beach where she played as a child.
rejected.remember: Pick a tense that suits the purpose, and stay in it unless the time changes.

a.q: A student is analysing a short story. Which sentence keeps its tense consistent in the usual way for analysis?
opts: The author uses short sentences, and this builds tension
The author used short sentences, and this builds tension
The author uses short sentences, and this built tension
The author used short sentences, and this will build tension
a.why: Both verbs, uses and builds, are in the present tense, which suits analysing a text. The other options switch tense in the middle with no change in time, which is the mistake the card warns about.
a.clue: Look for the sentence where every verb is in the same tense.

b.q: Jai is analysing a poem about a storm the poet lived through as a girl. Which sentence uses tense correctly?
opts: The poet repeats storm to show the fear she felt then
The poet repeated storm to show the fear she felt then
The poet repeats storm, which showed the fear she felt then
The poet repeats storm to show the fear she feels then
b.why: Repeats and show describe what the poem does, so they are in the present tense for analysis. Felt is past because the storm happened years earlier, which is a real change in time. Feels then is the tempting slip: it puts an earlier time in the present tense.
b.clue: Which verbs describe the poem, and which describe the storm years ago?

b.q: Jai is writing about a poem. Which sentence changes tense for a good reason?
opts: The poet repeats storm, which shows the fear she felt as a child
The poet repeated storm, which shows the fear she feels now
The poet repeats storm, which showed the fear she feels now
The poet repeated storm, which shows the fear she felt then
b.why: The analysis uses the present tense (repeats, shows), and the past tense felt refers to an earlier time, when she was a child. That is a real change in time. The other options switch tense with no change in time.
b.clue: Only one verb talks about an earlier time. The others analyse the poem.

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the only one with the precise detail 'as a child', which signals the earlier time, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea. The clue ('Only one verb talks about an earlier time') then points straight to it.

The example 'the writer builds suspense after the hero left home' is confusing. In literary analysis, events within the story are usually also described in the present tense ('after the hero leaves home'). Using a plot event as the 'earlier time' blurs the convention the card has just taught. An event before the text's time frame would be a clearer example.
